newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: U.S. honours dead from last Indochina War action.
newsitem.headline: U.S. honours dead from last Indochina War action.

text.p: U.S. Senator John McCain on Monday helped unveil a "long overdue" plaque honouring American servicemen killed 21 years ago off the Cambodian coast in the last military action of the Indochina War.

McCain and U.S. Ambassador to Cambodia Kenneth Quinn led the ceremony honouring the 18 marines, air force and navy personnel killed by Khmer Rouge soldiers in a disastrous attempt to rescue the crew of the container ship, Mayaguez, on May 15, 1975.

The black marble plaque also had the name of a U.S. Embassy marine security guard, Sergeant Charles Turberville, who was killed on September 26, 1971, by a bomb on a playing field near the mission. Those responsible were never brought to justice.

"Here in this embassy, in this tragic country, I think it's entirely appropriate we remember some who were sacrificed in a battle that never should have taken place and was largely forgotten," said the Arizona Republican on Veterans Day.

The Mayaguez and its crew of 39 were seized in Cambodian waters on May 12, 1975, by soldiers of Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge administration, which had taken power on April 17 and launched a terror reign that lasted almost four years and left more than one million people dead.

Helicopters on May 15, 1975, carried a force of marines on a rescue mission to the small island of Koh Tang, some 50 km (30 miles) off the Cambodian coast, in the mistaken belief that the Mayaguez crew was being held there.
By the time the U.S. commanders in Thailand realised the crew had been released elsewhere, three helicopters had been downed after running into fire from a Khmer Rouge garrison.

The rescue force pulled out, leaving a three-man fire team still alive on the island. They are among the 18 servicemen killed and all still missing from the action, most of them on one helicopter blown apart by a rocket propelled grenade.

U.S. military teams have made a number of missions to Koh Tang since late 1991 and last year recovered human remains and other signs of the fighting. The remains are undergoing forensic tests to try to identity them.
McCain, who spent several years as a prisoner of war after being shot down over Hanoi in 1967, described the unveiling of the plaque as "a long overdue tribute to their honour".

Monday's moving ceremony at the ambassador's residence was attended by Cambodian government officials, including co-Defence Ministers Tea Banh and Tea Chamrath, and Brigadier General Dennis Krupp of the marine corp.

McCain said the Cambodian government had been cooperative on the issue of prisoners and service personnel missing in action. There are still more than 2,000 U.S. servicemen listed as missing in action in Indochina since 1975, mostly in Vietnam and Laos, but with more than 70 in Cambodia.
